title: Mentoring & Peer Observation

pts: A structured peer observation has a clear, pre-agreed focus — a specific technique or question, not a general 'how did it go' impression.
This connects directly to Unit 67's action-research evidence-gathering, with a colleague's observation as one further data source.
Structure protects the observed teacher from vague, unfocused criticism and gives the observer a genuinely useful task.

items: The observed teacher chooses one focus: for example, teacher questions, instructions, wait time, or who speaks in pair work.
Together, choose or design a simple observation task for that focus (Wajnryb 1992).
The observer records only what the task asks for, without judging.
The observer gives the completed sheet to the teacher before any discussion.
The teacher reads it first and notes what surprises them.
If a colleague cannot visit, the teacher records audio of the lesson (with permission) and a colleague uses the task on the recording.
An action researcher (Unit 67) uses a colleague’s observation as one evidence source.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An observation task on teacher questions (written for this book):

lines: Write down every question the teacher asks. Mark each one D (display: the teacher knows the answer) or R (referential: a real question). Note the wait time in seconds.
What’s the past of ‘go’? D, 1 second.
What did you do on Sunday, Meena? R, 4 seconds.

blocks.x: The teacher sees a pattern that no general comment could show: 22 display questions and 3 referential ones.

body: Purpose: to show focused rather than general observation. Content: an observer at the back of a classroom holding a magnifying glass over one element (speech bubbles from the teacher); the rest of the room is lightly drawn. Style: warm classroom scene. Board version: a circle around one word.

items: Google Forms or Google Sheets (free) for simple tally observation sheets.

blocks.x: A printed or hand-drawn task sheet on a clipboard.

pts: A brief pre-observation conversation establishes the specific focus and context the observer should attend to.
A post-observation conversation, led by questions rather than unsolicited verdicts, supports the observed teacher's own reflective process.
This mirrors good feedback principles from Unit 8 and Unit 43, applied to professional, rather than learner, feedback.

v: The agreed focus; the observation record

items: Pre-observation (10 minutes): the teacher explains the class, the lesson aim and the focus; the observer asks clarifying questions only.
Agree where the observer will sit and whether learners will be told why.
Post-observation: start with the teacher’s own account of the lesson.
The observer shares the data, then asks questions rather than giving verdicts.
The teacher names one thing to keep and one thing to try.
Use a question card (see model language) until the question-led style becomes natural.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: A: How did you feel the questioning went?
B: Fine, I thought. They answered quickly.
A: Here’s the record. What do you notice?
B: Nearly all display questions. And the wait time is short.
A: What might happen if you waited longer after a real question?
B: More of them might answer. Especially the quieter ones.

blocks.x: The observed teacher reaches the insight; the observer provides evidence and questions. This mirrors good feedback to learners in Unit 8 and Unit 43.

body: Purpose: to show observation as a sequence, not a single visit. Content: three panels: two teachers talking before the lesson; one teacher teaching while another takes notes; the two talking afterwards over a sheet of paper. Style: comic-strip layout. Board version: three boxes with arrows.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared pre-observation note.

blocks.x: A printed question card for the observer.

pts: A mentoring relationship provides sustained, structured support over time, distinct from a single one-off observation.
Effective mentoring balances genuine support with honest, constructive challenge — echoing this series' own tone throughout.
New teachers particularly benefit from mentoring that addresses both technique and the emotional demands of early-career teaching.

items: Mentor and mentee meet and discuss the mentee’s hopes and worries for the first term.
Agree on how often to meet, for how long and where.
Agree on two or three development goals, including at least one about well-being or workload.
Agree on confidentiality: what stays between them and what, if anything, is reported.
Review the agreement after six weeks.
In a DIET, pair each pre-service trainee with a school-based mentor for the whole practicum.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A mentoring agreement (written for this book):

lines: We will meet every second Friday for 30 minutes in the library.
Goals: (1) giving clearer instructions; (2) managing noise in group work in Class 7; (3) finding a sustainable marking routine.
Confidentiality: our conversations are private; the mentor will not report on the mentee’s performance to the head teacher.

blocks.x: Separating mentoring from evaluation lets a new teacher admit difficulties without fear. Hobson et al. (2009) note that conflating the two roles can damage the relationship.

body: Purpose: to suggest sustained support. Content: two teachers walking side by side along a path marked with milestones (‘week 1’, ‘week 6’, ‘term 2’); the more experienced one points ahead but lets the other lead. Style: gentle illustration. Board version: a path with three marks.

items: Google Calendar (free) for regular meeting reminders.

blocks.x: A signed paper agreement in both teachers’ files.

pts: Being an excellent teacher doesn't automatically confer skill at mentoring — that's a distinct, learnable skill set of its own.
Effective mentors ask good questions and support the mentee's own problem-solving, rather than simply prescribing their own preferred solutions.
This connects to Unit 48's teacher-as-advisor principle, applied to mentoring a colleague rather than a learner.

v: Short written scenarios; a list of question stems

items: In threes, one person is mentee, one mentor and one observer.
The mentee describes a real or scenario problem in two minutes.
The mentor may only ask questions for five minutes, with no advice.
The observer notes the types of question used.
Rotate roles and discuss: when would a direct suggestion be appropriate?
Practise Freeman’s (1982) three approaches: directive, alternative (offering options) and non-directive, on the same problem.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: What were you hoping would happen?
What did you notice the learners doing?
What options can you see?
What would a small first step look like?
What support would help you try that?

blocks.x: Excellent teaching and excellent mentoring use different skills. Like the teacher as adviser to autonomous learners in Unit 48, the mentor’s task is to strengthen the other person’s own problem-solving.

body: Purpose: to highlight a questioning stance. Content: a mentor’s speech bubble containing a large question mark, and a mentee’s thought bubble with a lightbulb forming. Style: minimal. Board version: a question mark and a lightbulb.

items: None needed; this is a spoken practice task.

blocks.x: Question stems written on a card.

body: When you feel the urge to give advice, ask one more question first. If the mentee still asks for your view, offer two options rather than one answer, so the choice stays theirs.

pts: Lesson study has a group of teachers collaboratively plan, observe, and refine a single lesson together across multiple cycles.
This combines action research's cyclical structure (Unit 67) with genuinely shared, rather than individual, professional investigation.
The collaborative planning stage often surfaces valuable disagreement and diverse expertise a solo planning process would miss.

v: Three meetings of 45 minutes plus two lessons
A shared learning goal; a common class level

items: The group agrees a goal, for example: ‘Learners give reasons, not just opinions, in speaking.’
They plan one research lesson together in detail, predicting how learners will respond at each stage.
One teacher teaches it; the others observe learners, not the teacher, each following two or three learners.
In the post-lesson discussion, observers report what learners did and said.
The group revises the lesson and another teacher teaches it to a different class.
Invite a DIET lecturer or experienced colleague as a ‘knowledgeable other’ to comment at the final discussion (Lewis 2002).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: From a post-lesson discussion (written for this book):

lines: A: My two learners gave opinions quickly but stopped at ‘because’.
B: Mine used ‘because’ in Telugu and then gave up in English.

blocks.x: C: So the problem is the English for reasons, not the thinking. Shall we add a ‘because’ phrase bank before the task in version two? Planning together surfaces disagreement early. Observing learners rather than the teacher makes the discussion less personal and more useful.

body: Purpose: to show collaborative planning, teaching and revision. Content: a cycle with four teachers around a table (‘plan’), one teaching while three watch learners (‘teach and observe’), the group talking (‘reflect’), and a revised plan (‘re-teach’). Style: warm, diverse Indian staff room. Board version: a four-part circle.

items: Google Docs (free) for the shared lesson plan with comments.

blocks.x: A single printed plan annotated by each teacher in a different colour.

body: In Japan the practice is called jugyō kenkyū, literally ‘lesson study’ or ‘lesson research’. Stigler and Hiebert (1999) brought it to wide international attention through their comparison of mathematics teaching in several countries.

pts: Peer observation can feel exposing; building institutional norms of low-stakes, developmental (not evaluative) observation reduces this barrier.
This connects to Unit 22's classroom-climate principles, applied to the professional, adult learning environment among colleagues.
Starting with observation of willing volunteers, rather than mandatory rollout, often builds this culture more sustainably.

v: A staff list; a simple observation invitation

items: Announce a voluntary ‘open door’ week in which teachers invite colleagues to see one lesson.
Begin with two or three willing volunteers, including a senior teacher who invites observation first.
Use only focused, developmental observation tasks; keep all notes with the observed teacher.
After the week, share what participants learned (with permission), not what was ‘wrong’.
Repeat each term, inviting new volunteers.
In a school with a single English teacher, arrange cross-school visits through the cluster resource centre.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Open-door week, 12–16 August. I’m trying to increase wait time after questions in Class 8. You’re welcome to watch any of my periods on Tuesday or Thursday and count my wait time for me. I’ll return the favour.

blocks.x: When senior staff invite observation first, the message is that observation is for learning, not judgement. Unit 22 applied similar principles of trust and safety to learners.

body: Purpose: to symbolize low-stakes, voluntary observation. Content: a classroom door propped open with a small sign ‘Visitors welcome: focus on wait time’; a colleague with a notebook smiles at the door. Style: friendly. Board version: a door with a sign.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a simple sign-up schedule.

blocks.x: A sign-up sheet on the staff-room notice board.

pts: Peer mentoring between similarly-experienced colleagues, and even reverse mentoring (newer teachers sharing fresh perspectives), both have real value.
This connects to Unit 25's principled eclecticism — even experienced teachers benefit from fresh challenge to settled assumptions.
A mentoring culture limited only to formal senior-to-junior relationships misses much of this potential value.

v: A list of skills each person can offer and wants to learn

items: Each teacher writes two things they could share and two they would like to learn.
Match pairs by complementary lists, not only by seniority.
Each pair agrees one focus for a term.
Pairs observe or co-plan once a month.
At the end of term, each partner names one assumption the other challenged.
A newly qualified teacher shares a digital tool or a recent training idea with a senior colleague.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A matched pair (written for this book):

lines: Mrs Lakshmi (25 years): offers large-class management and exam-paper design; wants to learn to use short videos.
Mr Arjun (2 years): offers video and phone-based tools; wants to learn to manage noise in group work.
A: I used to think group work in Class 10 was a waste of time before the board exam.
B: And I thought my video clips were enough on their own. You showed me the pre-listening task matters more.

blocks.x: Unit 25’s principled eclecticism applies here: fresh eyes help even experienced teachers question settled habits.

body: Purpose: to show mentoring as reciprocal. Content: two teachers of different ages exchanging items (a phone and a chalk-stick) across a table, with a double-headed arrow between them. Style: warm, respectful. Board version: two figures and a double arrow.

items: WhatsApp (free) for a small, focused pair channel.

blocks.x: A shared notebook passed between partners.

pts: Occasional formal training has limited lasting impact without ongoing structures like mentoring and peer observation to sustain and apply it.
This connects mentoring and observation directly to Unit 9's reflective practice as its natural, sustained, collaborative extension.
A durable professional development culture treats collaboration as ongoing infrastructure, not a periodic special event.

blocks.x: A professional development map for the year

v: School leaders, DIET faculty, teacher groups
The school calendar; current training schedule

items: List all formal training teachers will attend this year.
For each, plan a follow-up structure: a peer observation, a mentoring meeting, or a lesson study cycle within four weeks.
Set regular slots in the timetable for collaborative work, even 30 minutes a fortnight.
Assign a coordinator to keep the calendar going.
Review the map at the end of the year with the staff.
Link the map to the school’s action research programme (Unit 67) and to teachers’ reflective practice (Unit 72).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An annual map (written for this book):

lines: July: state training on reading comprehension → August: peer observation of one reading lesson each.
September: DIET workshop on speaking tasks → October: lesson study cycle on a speaking lesson.
All year: fortnightly mentoring for two new teachers; monthly teacher learning circle.

blocks.x: Training alone rarely changes practice for long. Ongoing, collaborative follow-up is what turns an idea from a workshop into a habit in the classroom (Richards and Farrell 2005).

body: Purpose: to show development as ongoing infrastructure. Content: a year-long timeline with training events as large dots and many small linked dots after each (observations, mentoring, lesson study) forming a continuous thread. Style: clean infographic. Board version: a line with large and small dots.

items: Google Calendar or Google Sheets (free) for a shared school development calendar.

blocks.x: A wall calendar in the staff room.

body: Invite one colleague to observe twenty minutes of your next lesson with a single focus you choose. Hold a ten-minute conversation afterwards in which your colleague may only ask questions. Then offer to do the same for them.

dek: Unit 68 of 100: extending individual reflective and research practice into genuinely collaborative professional development — through mentoring and structured peer observation.

aims.x: Most teachers spend their working lives alone with their classes. This unit shows how colleagues can make each other’s teaching visible in ways that are safe, focused and useful. It covers structured peer observation, the conversations before and after it, mentoring relationships and the skills they need, lesson study, and the conditions that let such practices last beyond a single training programme.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: plan a peer observation with a clear, agreed focus and a simple observation task;
conduct pre- and post-observation conversations led by questions;
describe what distinguishes mentoring from one-off observation;
use core mentoring skills: listening, questioning and supporting the mentee’s own problem-solving;
organize a short lesson study cycle with colleagues;
build a developmental, low-stakes culture of observation in a school or DIET;
set up peer and reverse mentoring as well as senior-to-junior mentoring;
plan structures that sustain professional development over years.

why: Why this matters. Teaching can be an isolating profession. Structured collaboration turns individual reflection and research into a shared, mutually reinforcing professional practice.

background.x: In many Indian schools, the only person who observes a teacher is an inspector, a head teacher or a resource person, and the purpose is evaluation. Teachers learn to perform for such visits. Developmental observation has a different purpose: to help the observed teacher see and understand their own teaching. Ruth Wajnryb (1992) showed how focused observation tasks can make observation a learning experience for both observer and observed. Jack Richards and Thomas Farrell (2005) describe peer observation, peer coaching, teaching portfolios and teacher support groups as complementary forms of professional development.

Mentoring has a long history in teacher education. Angi Malderez and Caroline Bodóczky (1999) describe the mentor as someone who supports a new teacher’s professional learning, not simply someone who demonstrates good practice. A review of research on mentoring beginning teachers found that it can support retention, confidence and practice, but that the quality of the relationship and the mentor’s preparation matter a great deal (Hobson et al. 2009). Donald Freeman (1982) distinguished directive, alternative and non-directive approaches to working with teachers, a distinction that remains useful for mentors deciding how much to tell and how much to ask.

Lesson study, developed in Japan, brings a group of teachers together to plan a ‘research lesson’, observe it being taught and revise it (Stigler and Hiebert 1999; Lewis 2002). It combines the cyclical structure of action research (Unit 67) with shared planning. It has attracted interest in many countries, including India, where several states and organizations have piloted it [VERIFY specific Indian lesson study initiatives before naming them].

NEP 2020 recommends that teachers have opportunities for continuous professional development and envisages mentoring for teachers, including a national mission for mentoring (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). DIETs, Block Resource Centres and Cluster Resource Centres already provide structures in which observation and mentoring can happen. Teachers can mentor in any shared language: a post-observation conversation in Kannada or Marathi about an English lesson is often deeper and more honest than one in a second language.

items: Observation record. A completed focused observation task with the teacher’s own notes on what it showed.
Conversation log. A short record of a question-led post-observation conversation, with the agreed ‘keep’ and ‘try’.
Mentoring agreement. A written agreement reviewed after six weeks, with progress on its goals.
Lesson study report. Two versions of a research lesson with the changes explained by observed learner behaviour.
When were you last observed for development rather than evaluation? How did it feel?
What would you most like a colleague to observe in your teaching?
Do you tend to tell or to ask when a colleague brings you a problem?
What could you learn from a colleague with less experience than you?
What structures in your school or DIET could support regular observation?
In which language do you and your colleagues talk most honestly about teaching?

perm: All observation tasks, agreements, invitations, maps and dialogues are written for this book; the observation task in point 1 is original, though inspired by the approach in Wajnryb (1992), and should not be presented as reproduced from it. Screenshots of Google Forms, Sheets, Docs, Calendar or WhatsApp require permission or replacement with original illustrations. Audio recordings of lessons need the consent of the school, the teacher and learners’ parents or guardians.

terms.def: Ways of working with teachers in mentoring and supervision: a directive mentor tells the teacher what to change, while a non-directive mentor listens and asks questions so the teacher reaches their own decisions (Freeman 1982).

A collaborative form of professional development, originating in Japan, in which teachers jointly plan a lesson, one teaches it while colleagues observe learners, and the group then discusses and revises the lesson.
A supportive professional relationship in which an experienced teacher guides a less experienced colleague through observation, discussion and shared reflection, rather than through evaluation alone.
A focused task given to an observer, such as recording teacher questions or learner talk time, so that the observation collects specific evidence rather than general impressions.
Teachers observing one another’s lessons for mutual learning rather than evaluation, usually with an agreed focus and a follow-up conversation.
The discussion after an observed lesson in which the observer and the teacher reflect together on the evidence collected, rather than on general impressions, and agree realistic next steps.
The discussion before an observed lesson in which the teacher and observer agree the lesson’s aims and the focus of observation.

In lesson study, a lesson planned in detail by a group of teachers, taught by one while the others observe learners’ responses, and then revised and often retaught (Stigler and Hiebert 1999; Lewis 2002).
Mentoring in which a less experienced or younger teacher supports a more senior colleague in an area of their own expertise, such as digital tools, while also learning from the relationship.
A group of teachers who meet regularly to learn together, share practice, observe each other and try out new ideas, such as a school or cluster-level group supported by a DIET.
